findings.finding: Stored replies run inside the job's terminal write next to the coalescing chunk writer. storeReply adds exactly two statements, the chat_owners stamp and the message insert, and only on the terminal write, because the chunk writer sends only non-terminal batches. The row-limit check runs in memory before the stamp and adds no statement.
findings.none: Proven by the reply-speed bench: base c28456d gave 119, 119, 119 worker statements per reply; the earlier build of this code gave 115, 121, 121 and 115, 115, 121, and this head gives 115, 121, 115 with first text at 402 to 424 ms. One coalesced write more or less moves the count by about six. The worker tests for chunks during a slow write, Stop mid-stream, and a lost worker plus retry pass at head.

findings.finding: Lock order after the merge. The claim now takes the attempt advisory lock first, and every writer of chats, chat_messages or deleted_chats.seq takes the chat_owners row last (update, requestCancellation, reconcile, deleteChat through purgeChat, and ChatRows.push). No lock cycle is reachable. A refused reply returns before the stamp, so it takes no lock.
findings.none: Walked every writer in jobs.ts and chats.ts; the order matches the stamp comment in chats.ts. A two-connection deadlock test needs a real Postgres, because PGlite runs one connection, so this stays at a walkthrough.

findings.finding: A reply over the message row limit (1,000,000 characters of text or of reasoning) was stored by storeReply, because the snapshot schema leaves both unbounded. ChatRows.pull decodes its page with syncPageSchema, so every later pull for that account answered 400, and the app's sync loop, which pulls before it pushes and swallows errors, stopped for good with no notice. storeReply now refuses that row, the rule messageRow already applies on the phone. Proven by running code: the new chats.test case fails with a 400 pull without the check and also with a text-only check, and a scratch run of the real JobRepository and ChatRows on PGlite now pulls with no error after a 1,000,005-character reply.

Refusing the row instead of truncating it. Truncation is ruled out because receiveMessage in archive.ts overwrites a known message's text with the pulled row, so a truncated server copy would cut the full reply on the phone that produced it. The cost of refusing: another phone holds that chat row until every message on its leaf path arrives (receiveChat in archive.ts), so a chat whose path runs through a refused reply does not appear on other phones.
findings.none: Accepted: it needs one reply of about 250k output tokens, and it is the same outcome the app already gives for any row it refuses itself. Checked by pointing at the lines, not by a run.

findings.finding: A message whose text holds a NUL character or an unpaired surrogate passes messageRowSchema on the phone, but ChatRows.push fails on it, because PostgreSQL jsonb refuses both. The phone keeps that row first in its outbox, and sync.ts retries the same batch and swallows the error, so every later upload from that phone stops with no notice. Pulls keep working. A scratch run of the real ChatRows on PGlite showed both failures: push threw 'unsupported Unicode escape sequence' for NUL and 'invalid input syntax for type json' for an unpaired surrogate.
findings.none: Minor, a documented limit. jobs.submit on main already refuses the same text, and no app code cuts saved text by UTF-16 index (the title uses a code-point spread), so only pasted input can reach it. Follow-up: add a well-formedness check to messageRowSchema and the chat title so the phone moves such a row to its unsynced list, and treat a repeated server refusal of a one-row batch as a refusal.

findings.finding: Lock order between ChatRows.push, storeReply and deleteChat. A delete that stamps first makes the waiting push's next statement see the tombstone; a delete that stamps second runs its DELETE after the push commits and removes those rows. Both orders end with no rows for the deleted chat.
findings.none: Walkthrough under READ COMMITTED agrees with the author's; the two-connection test still needs a real Postgres.
